common_name: Explosion in the Paint Factory Daylily (2025 Stout Medal Broken-Pattern Unusual-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Explosion in the Paint Factory carries an unusually vivid broken color pattern splashed irregularly over its petals.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Rich Howard and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2025, Explosion in the Paint Factory bears yellow flowers about seven inches across broken by irregular red streaks and splashes, with spatulate sepals and crispate, cascading petals that give each bloom a wild, painterly unpredictability from flower to flower. Scapes reach roughly 38 inches and each carries around 20 buds that open over a midseason display with some later rebloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Breathing in Snowflakes Daylily (2024 Stout Medal Cascading Lavender Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Breathing in Snowflakes is a fragrant diploid with dependable rebloom through the growing season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Heidi Douglas and introduced in 2016, Breathing in Snowflakes earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2024 for its cascading, fragrant, light lavender flowers roughly 6.5 inches across, marked by a darker lavender band encircling an almost white halo above a pale yellow throat that extends well onto the sepals. This diploid cultivar blooms on scapes around 29 inches tall in midseason and reblooms consistently through summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain heavy flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Isabelle Rose Daylily (2022 Stout Medal Diamond-Dusted Spider-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Isabelle Rose sends up unusually tall scapes and benefits from staking support in windy sites.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Ellen Laprise, introduced in 2009, and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2022, Isabelle Rose bears pale yellow, diamond-dusted flowers about seven inches across with lightly ruffled, cascading petals above an extended green throat. This dormant, fragrant diploid sends up exceptionally tall scapes to nearly five feet, towering above most daylily cultivars and making it a striking back-of-border accent. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: I Lava You Daylily (2020 Stout Medal Red-Orange Unusual-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; I Lava You carries a heavy bud count for a long midseason display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Sandy Holmes, registered in 2009, and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2020, I Lava You bears clean, bright red-orange flowers up to nine inches across with a paler orange watermark bleeding out into the petals, an unusual-form tetraploid carrying around 24 buds across five branches per scape. Scapes stand roughly 44 inches tall and flower in a heavy midseason flush. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Entwined in the Vine Daylily (2018 Stout Medal Patterned Lavender-Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Entwined in the Vine is very fragrant and reblooms well through the summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Emmerich in 2007 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2018, Entwined in the Vine bears lavender-pink flowers about eight inches across patterned with a multicolored lavender-violet eye and an edge trimmed in ivory-gold above a yellow-green throat. This very fragrant, evergreen tetraploid blooms in midseason with reliable rebloom through summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Heavenly United We Stand Daylily (2017 Stout Medal Giant Blood-Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Heavenly United We Stand performs best where winters deliver a sustained cold dormancy period.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Gossard in 2009 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2017, Heavenly United We Stand produces massive, sun-fast blood-red flowers up to nine inches wide above a clean green throat, carried on tall scapes around 51 inches with roughly 36 buds across seven branches. This dormant tetraploid is best suited to regions with a sustained winter chill and flowers in a bold midseason display beginning around mid-June. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Dorothy and Toto Daylily (2015 Stout Medal Double-Form Rose-Peach Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Dorothy and Toto produces fully double blooms on nearly every flower rather than occasionally like many double-form cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Katisue Herrington, registered in 2003, and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2015, Dorothy and Toto bears fully double, fragrant flowers about six inches across in a rose, peach, and cream blend above a green throat. This tetraploid cultivar blooms consistently double on nearly every scape, opening on stems around 30 inches tall through a midseason display. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Heavenly Angel Ice Daylily (2013 Stout Medal White Spider-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Heavenly Angel Ice is among the closest approaches to a true white daylily achieved in modern breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Jamie Gossard in 2004 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2013, Heavenly Angel Ice bears large, near-white self flowers over eight inches across above a green-yellow throat, with narrow, twisting, crispate petals typical of a daylily of unusual form. This dormant diploid blooms in a midseason-to-late display and reblooms over the summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Carnival in Mexico Daylily (2012 Stout Medal Red-Eyed Rose Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Carnival in Mexico shows a bold, saturated eyezone that intensifies in cooler weather.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Santa Lucia in 2000 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2012, Carnival in Mexico bears pale, veined rose flowers about seven inches across marked by a very large, deep red eyezone above a green throat. This dormant tetraploid carries around 22 buds across three branches per scape and blooms on stems roughly 30 inches tall in a strong midseason display. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: J.T. Davis Daylily (2010 Stout Medal Ruffled Gold-Edged Blush Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; J.T. Davis shows good rust resistance and is both pod and pollen fertile, making it a popular hybridizing parent.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Larry Grace at Graceland Gardens and introduced in 1999, J.T. Davis earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2010 for its fragrant, light yellow-pink blush blooms edged in ruffled gold above a green throat. This evergreen tetraploid blooms in midseason with dependable rebloom and has proven a widely used hybridizing parent, with several hundred registered offspring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Skinwalker Daylily (2009 Stout Medal Lavender Spider-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Skinwalker previously won the Harris-Olson Spider Award for Best Spider in 2004.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Roberts and introduced in 1997, Skinwalker earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2009 for its lavender-blend, spider-form flowers over eight inches across above a green throat, with narrow petals and sepals that twist gracefully as they open. This dormant diploid blooms on scapes around 31 inches tall through midseason. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Lavender Blue Baby Daylily (2007 Stout Medal Watermark-Eye Lavender Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Lavender Blue Baby is a stunning rebloomer valued for its crisp watermark eye pattern.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Carpenter in 1996 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2007, Lavender Blue Baby bears fragrant, lavender-pink flowers about 5.5 inches wide centered with a vivid lavender-blue watermark eye above a green throat. This dormant diploid opens its flowers early in the midseason and reblooms strongly through summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Brocaded Gown Daylily (1989 Stout Medal Textured Lemon-Cream Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Brocaded Gown shows a distinctive seersucker-like petal texture unusual among lemon-cream daylilies.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Millikan, registered in 1979, and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1989, Brocaded Gown bears large, six-inch, creamy lemon self flowers above a chartreuse throat, with a lightly crinkled, seersucker-like petal texture that sets it apart from smoother-petaled cultivars. This semi-evergreen diploid blooms in an early-midseason flush and reblooms later in summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Clarence Simon Daylily (1975 Stout Medal Pink-Melon Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Clarence Simon also received the Lenington All-American Award in 1976 for its outstanding garden performance across diverse climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by MacMillan in 1966 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1975, Clarence Simon bears clear pink-melon self flowers about six inches across on scapes roughly 28 inches tall. This evergreen diploid blooms in midseason and reblooms, and its exceptional garden reliability across a wide range of climates also earned it the Lenington All-American Award the following year. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Lavender Flight Daylily (1973 Stout Medal Deep Lavender Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Lavender Flight was one of Edna Spalding's three Stout Medal-winning introductions, alongside Luxury Lace and Martha Adams.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Edna Spalding in 1963 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1973, Lavender Flight bears lightly fragrant, deep lavender self flowers over six inches across on scapes around 34 inches tall. This semi-evergreen cultivar blooms in an early-midseason flush and was among the introductions that helped establish true lavender and orchid tones as a serious color class in daylily breeding. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Neal Berrey Daylily (1995 Stout Medal Rose-Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Neal Berrey has proven a popular hybridizing parent behind numerous later rose-pink daylily cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Sarah Sikes in 1985 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1995, Neal Berrey bears rose-pink, extended flowers about five inches across above a green throat, held on compact scapes under two feet tall. This semi-evergreen diploid blooms in midseason and has been widely used as a hybridizing parent for later rose-pink cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records
